# Oregonator (Belousov-Zhabotinsky)

`oregonator` · *Field & Noyes, 1974*

## Introduction

The Oregonator is a model of a real chemical clock. Mix the right reagents
in a beaker of sulphuric acid and the solution turns from colourless to
yellowish and back, over and over. This is the
*Belousov–Zhabotinsky reaction* (BZ reaction for short), a famous
chemical oscillator. The BZ reaction is not one reaction but, in the book's
words, "a family of catalyzed redox reactions". The Oregonator boils it down to five reactions
among three changing species, `X`, `Y` and `Z`, which is still enough to make
the concentrations cycle.

The book describes the BZ oscillation as three stages that feed into each
other. First, a metal ion such as cerium is oxidised from Ce(III) to Ce(IV)
by an autocatalytic process, one whose product (bromous acid) speeds up its
own production; the solution turns yellow. Second, the Ce(IV) is reduced back
to Ce(III), and this releases bromide ions, which inhibit the first stage;
the solution clears. Third, the bromide is used up, the brake comes off, and
the first stage can start again. In the Oregonator, `X` is the autocatalyst
(bromous acid, HBrO₂), `Y` the inhibitor (bromide, Br⁻) and `Z` the oxidised
metal ion (Ce(IV)), whose concentration is the colour one sees.

The model was devised by Richard Field and Richard Noyes at the University
of Oregon and published in 1974 in a paper titled
"Oscillations in chemical systems. IV. Limit cycle behavior in a model of a
real chemical reaction". According to Field's own review article (2007) it
is a reduction of the detailed BZ mechanism that Field, Kőrös and Noyes had
proposed earlier (the *FKN mechanism*), and the simplest model that is still
chemically realistic. A *limit cycle*, as in the title, is an oscillation
that the system settles into from any nearby start, with its own fixed
period and amplitude.

It is a kinetic simulation model: a fixed list of reactions with mass-action
rates, meant to be turned into differential equations and integrated. No new
species ever appear, so it is not constructive. Banzhaf and Yamamoto use it
in their chapter on wet artificial chemistries, in the section on
reaction-diffusion computers (book §19.3.3). There the point is what happens
when the BZ reagents are *not* stirred: waves of colour spread through the
dish as rings and spirals, and those waves can carry and process
information. The book simulated such waves with the Oregonator on a
hexagonal grid (its figure 19.20).

Among the catalog's other oscillators, the [Brusselator](brusselator.md) is
an invented, idealised scheme with only two changing species, while the
Oregonator models an actual chemical reaction; the
[Repressilator](repressilator.md) is the biological counterpart, an
oscillator built from genes in bacteria. The Oregonator's neighbours in the
wet family, such as [Adleman's DNA computation](dna-hpp.md) and the
[DNA automaton](dna-automaton.md), compute with molecules in a test tube;
the BZ medium computes with waves in space.

## How it works

### The five reactions

```
A + Y -> X          (k1)  bromide Y is consumed, making X
X + Y -> P          (k2)  X and bromide destroy each other
B + X -> 2 X + Z    (k3)  autocatalysis: X makes more X, and oxidises the metal (Z)
2 X -> Q            (k4)  two X meet and are removed
Z -> f Y            (k5)  the oxidised metal is reduced, releasing f bromides
```

Each `k` is a *rate constant*. Under *mass action*, the law the book uses, a
reaction runs at its rate constant times the product of its reactant
concentrations: `B + X -> 2 X + Z` runs at `k3 × [B] × [X]` (square brackets
mean concentration), and `2 X -> Q` at `k4 × [X]²`.

`A` and `B` are *buffered*: the book says they "are continuously
replenished such that their concentrations remain constant". They stand for
bulk reagents that, in Field's words, "are normally present in much
higher concentrations" than `X`, `Y` and `Z`, and can be taken as constant
over a few oscillations. `P` and `Q` are waste products;
they never react again, so they do not affect the dynamics. That leaves
three species that actually change: `X`, `Y` and `Z`.

The number `f` is a *stoichiometric factor*: how many bromide ions each
reduced metal ion releases, on average. The book says it "is meant to make
the Oregonator scheme more generic, and can be set to one in its simplest
case". It need not be a whole number, and it is the model's main control
knob: it sets how strongly the brake acts.

The book maps the stages onto the reactions as follows. Reactions 3 and 4
are the first stage: `X` multiplies and oxidises the metal, and reaction 4
stops `X` from growing without limit. Reaction 5 is the second stage: `Z`
turns into the inhibitor `Y`. Reactions 1 and 2 are the third stage: `Y` is
consumed until it can no longer hold `X` down.

### One cycle, step by step

Here is one period of the default network (the book's rate constants,
`f = 1`, `A = B = 1`), integrated with the script under "Using it". The
table starts at a peak of `X` and samples every 0.4 time units:

```
t= 93.10   X=0.950   Y=0.587   Z=6.376
t= 93.50   X=0.836   Y=0.727   Z=7.258
t= 93.90   X=0.618   Y=0.932   Z=7.245
t= 94.30   X=0.423   Y=1.152   Z=6.532
t= 94.70   X=0.318   Y=1.294   Z=5.562
t= 95.10   X=0.298   Y=1.262   Z=4.722
t= 95.50   X=0.346   Y=1.076   Z=4.213
t= 95.90   X=0.485   Y=0.823   Z=4.177
t= 96.30   X=0.746   Y=0.612   Z=4.833
t= 96.70   X=0.944   Y=0.572   Z=6.113
t= 97.10   X=0.873   Y=0.691   Z=7.150
```

Read it as a chase. At `t = 93.1` the autocatalyst `X` is at its peak and
bromide `Y` is low, so reaction 3 is running fast and `Z` (the colour) is
still climbing; it peaks around `t = 93.7`. All that `Z` is being turned
into bromide by reaction 5, so `Y` rises, and bromide destroys `X`
(reaction 2): `X` falls. By `t = 95` bromide is at its highest and `X` at its
lowest; with little `X` left, little new `Z` is made, and `Z` fades. Now the
bromide is consumed faster than it is replaced, `Y` drops, and once it is
low enough `X` takes off again. The next peak of `X` arrives about 3.7 time
units after the first, and the cycle repeats.

Two features make this work. The autocatalytic step lets `X` grow in a
burst; and the brake acts with a delay, because bromide is not made by `X`
directly but only after passing through `Z`. Field's review calls the
Oregonator an activator–inhibitor system with "a delayed negative feedback
loop", and names `Z` as the inhibitor species; the book names `Y`,
the molecule that does the inhibiting. Both describe the same loop.

### Steady state, stability and `f`

Setting the three rates of change to zero gives the *steady state*, the
mixture at which production and consumption balance. At `f = 1` it is
`X ≈ 0.584`, `Y ≈ 0.854`, `Z ≈ 5.84`. The cycle above circles it without
ever landing on it, because the steady state is *unstable*: a small
disturbance grows, in widening oscillations, until it reaches the limit
cycle. Whether the steady state is stable depends on `f`, the strength of
the brake. With little bromide per metal ion the system comes to rest with
`X` high; with a lot, it comes to rest with `X` held low. Only in between
does it oscillate. The switch between resting and oscillating at each end of
that range is a *Hopf bifurcation*. A linear stability analysis of the
default rate constants, done for this page (not from the book), puts the
range at `0.881 < f < 1.458`; the runs under "Using it" confirm it.

### Space

Everything so far assumes a stirred, uniform solution. The book's patterns
come from adding *diffusion*: each species spreads from high to low
concentration at a rate set by its diffusion coefficient `D`, while reacting
locally. This *reaction-diffusion* system is solved on a grid of cells, each
running the five reactions and exchanging molecules with its neighbours; the
book used a hexagonal grid and started the waves from random drops of `Z`.
The book gives neither the diffusion coefficients nor the grid spacing.

### What Chemart supplies

Chemart generates the network: the five reactions with their rate
constants, the buffered species, and a record of the spatial setting. It
does not integrate the equations or simulate space; the examples below do
that with a few lines of NumPy and SciPy. One detail: a reaction cannot
release 1.5 molecules, so a fractional `f` is written as two reactions with
whole numbers of products that together give exactly the same rate
equations. The formal specification below summarises the model.

### Formal specification

Banzhaf and Yamamoto describe every artificial chemistry by three things (book §2.3): the set of possible molecules **S**, the reaction rules **R** that transform them, and the reactor algorithm **A** that decides which reactions happen, and when. For this chemistry:

**S — molecules** (*explicit* — listed up front). A, B (buffered reactants), X (autocatalyst, HBrO2), Y (inhibitor, Br-), Z (oxidised metal ion, e.g. Ce(IV)), P, Q (products)

**R — reactions** (*explicit* — listed reaction by reaction; molecules per reaction: 1, 2). A + Y --k1--&gt; X ; X + Y --k2--&gt; P ; B + X --k3--&gt; 2X + Z ; 2X --k4--&gt; Q ; Z --k5--&gt; f Y

**A — reactor**: `ode` (deterministic rate equations: concentrations change continuously in time); or `lattice-2d` (a two-dimensional grid on which only neighbours interact).

*How the population is bounded:* A and B buffered; reaction-diffusion on a grid for spatial patterns

### Using it in Chemart

Every parameter at its default:

```python
import chemart
net = chemart.generate_network("oregonator", seed=1)
print(net.summary())
```

```
oregonator: 7 species, 5 reactions, status=complete
provides: catalysts, initial-state, rate-constants, space, stoichiometry, topology
seed: 1
extras: buffered, space
```

Its first reactions (`net.reactions`):

```
A + Y -> X  [mass-action k=1.0]
X + Y -> P  [mass-action k=10.0]
B + X -> 2 X + Z  [mass-action k=10.0]
2 X -> Q  [mass-action k=2.5]
Z -> Y  [mass-action k=1.0]
```

The default call above builds the network of the book's figure 19.20:
`k1 = k5 = 1`, `k2 = k3 = 10`, `k4 = 2.5`. The book does not give `f`, `A`,
`B` or the diffusion coefficients, so Chemart sets `f = 1` (the "simplest
case") and `A = B = 1`, and every diffusion coefficient to 1. The network
has no randomness; the `seed` changes nothing.

`net.initial_state` holds only `A = B = 1`, so `X`, `Y` and `Z` start at
zero. Every reaction then has a zero rate and nothing ever happens: a
simulation must seed some `Y` (or `X`). `net.extras` has two fields:
`buffered`, naming `A` and `B`, which a simulator must hold constant, and
`space`, with the `lattice` (`"hexagonal"` or `"square"`) and the
`diffusion` coefficient of each species, for whoever builds a spatial
simulation.

#### Oscillation at the book's constants

This script integrates the generated network, holding the buffered species
fixed, and prints the cycle shown in "How it works":

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.integrate import solve_ivp

import chemart


def simulate(net, t_end, start, n=20001):
    ids, R, P = net.matrices()
    R = R.toarray()
    S = (P.toarray() - R).astype(float)
    k = np.array([r.rate["k"] for r in net.reactions])
    held = [ids.index(s) for s in net.extras["buffered"]]
    x0 = np.array([start.get(s, net.initial_state.get(s, 0.0)) for s in ids])

    def rhs(t, x):
        v = k * np.prod(x[:, None] ** R, axis=0)  # mass action
        dx = S @ v
        dx[held] = 0.0  # A and B are buffered
        return dx

    t = np.linspace(0, t_end, n)
    sol = solve_ivp(rhs, (0, t_end), x0, t_eval=t, method="LSODA", rtol=1e-9, atol=1e-12)
    return t, dict(zip(ids, sol.y))


net = chemart.generate_network("oregonator", seed=1)  # the book's constants, f = 1
t, x = simulate(net, 100, start={"Y": 1.0}, n=100001)  # X, Y, Z start at 0: give Y a push
i0 = np.searchsorted(t, 90)
i0 += np.argmax(x["X"][i0:i0 + 4000])  # start at a peak of X
for i in range(i0, i0 + 4001, 400):
    print(f"t={t[i]:6.2f}   X={x['X'][i]:.3f}   Y={x['Y'][i]:.3f}   Z={x['Z'][i]:.3f}")
```

Its output is the table in "How it works". The run takes about two seconds.

#### Scanning `f`

With the same `simulate`, run each value of `f` to `t = 400` and print the
range of `Z` over the last 100 time units. A range of zero means the run has
come to rest at the steady state:

```python
for f in (0.85, 0.9, 1.0, 1.2, 1.4, 1.5, 2.0):
    t, x = simulate(chemart.generate_network("oregonator", f=f), 400, start={"Y": 1.0}, n=40001)
    Z = x["Z"][t >= 300]
    print(f"f={f}: Z from {Z.min():.2f} to {Z.max():.2f}")
```

```
f=0.85: Z from 7.16 to 7.16
f=0.9: Z from 5.59 to 7.59
f=1.0: Z from 4.12 to 7.36
f=1.2: Z from 3.36 to 6.08
f=1.4: Z from 3.21 to 4.45
f=1.5: Z from 3.46 to 3.46
f=2.0: Z from 2.55 to 2.55
```

The oscillation exists between `f = 0.85` and `f = 1.5`, as the stability
analysis predicts, with the widest swing near `f = 1`. More bromide per
metal ion also lowers the resting level of `Z`. In separate runs the period
stayed close to 3.7 time units across the whole window (3.59 at `f = 0.9`,
3.70 at `f = 1.2`).

#### A fractional `f`

```python
print(chemart.generate_network("oregonator", f=1.5).to_text())
```

```
A + Y -> X  [mass-action k=1.0]
X + Y -> P  [mass-action k=10.0]
B + X -> 2 X + Z  [mass-action k=10.0]
2 X -> Q  [mass-action k=2.5]
Z -> Y  [mass-action k=0.5]
Z -> 2 Y  [mass-action k=0.5]
```

`Z` still disappears at total rate `k5 = 1`, and releases on average
`0.5 × 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 1.5` bromides, so the rate equations are those of
`Z -> 1.5 Y`. For `f` below 1 one of the two reactions is `Z -> ∅`, which
releases nothing. The other parameters, in the table below, are the five
rate constants, the buffered concentrations and the two spatial settings.

#### Parameters

Pass any of these as keyword arguments to `generate_network`. The *role* column says what a parameter controls: `structural` (which molecules and reactions exist), `kinetic` (rates), `thermodynamic` (energies, temperature), `population` (sizes, budgets, initial state), `spatial`, `stochastic` or `selection`. *range* gives the values used in the published work.

| name | type | default | role | what it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `k1` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | A + Y -&gt; X <br>≥ `0` |
| `k2` | `float` | `10.0` | kinetic | X + Y -&gt; P <br>≥ `0` |
| `k3` | `float` | `10.0` | kinetic | B + X -&gt; 2X + Z <br>≥ `0` |
| `k4` | `float` | `2.5` | kinetic | 2X -&gt; Q <br>≥ `0` |
| `k5` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | Z -&gt; f Y <br>≥ `0` |
| `f` | `float` | `1.0` | kinetic | stoichiometric factor of inhibitor regeneration; the key bifurcation parameter <br>≥ `0` |
| `A` | `float` | `1.0` | population | buffered concentration of A <br>≥ `0` |
| `B` | `float` | `1.0` | population | buffered concentration of B <br>≥ `0` |
| `D` | `dict` | `{'X': 1.0, 'Y': 1.0, 'Z': 1.0}` | spatial | diffusion coefficient per species for the reaction-diffusion setting |
| `lattice` | `enum` | `hexagonal` | spatial | grid used for reaction-diffusion (the book's patterns use a hexagonal grid) <br>one of `square`, `hexagonal` |

### Implementation decisions

The sources leave gaps, and sometimes contradict each other or the book. Each such case, and how Chemart resolved it, is listed here: read these before quoting a number from this page.

??? note "3 decisions"

    - Rate constants are the book's (figure 19.20). f, the buffered concentrations A and B, and the diffusion coefficients are not given; defaults are f = 1, A = B = 1, D = 1.
    - A real f cannot be an integer stoichiometric coefficient. Z -&gt; f Y is emitted as Z -&gt; floor(f) Y at rate k5 (1 - frac(f)) plus Z -&gt; (floor(f)+1) Y at rate k5 frac(f), which gives exactly the same rate equations.
    - Space is recorded in extras.space (lattice, diffusion); A and B are listed in extras.buffered.

## Results

**A model of a real reaction that oscillates.** The title of Field and
Noyes (1974) states their result: limit-cycle behaviour in a model of a
real chemical reaction. Field's review (2007) summarises what the model has shown
since. With realistic rate constants, the steady state is unstable in a
roughly triangular region of the plane of the two adjustable parameters (the
rate of reaction 5 and `f`); as that rate goes to zero the unstable range
approaches `0.5 < f < 1 + √2`. The borders are Hopf bifurcations, and near
them the oscillations appear and vanish abruptly at large amplitude, "in
keeping with the observation that the BZ oscillations appear full blown at
low-f and disappear abruptly from large-amplitude at high-f". The same review
reports that the Oregonator is excitable and shows bursting near those
borders. An *excitable* system rests at a stable state but answers a large
enough push with one full excursion before returning.

Chemart reproduces the qualitative result with the book's constants: an
oscillation that exists only in a window of `f`, found here to be
`0.881 < f < 1.458`. The window is narrower than Field's, and the book's
constants are far from the chemical ones. Written in Field's scaled variables, they give a time-scale ratio
`ε = k5 / (k3·B) = 0.1`, where the real chemistry has about 0.0099, and
`q = 2·k1·k4·A / (k2·k3·B) = 0.05`, where it has about 0.000076 (these two
values for the book's constants are computed for this page). The only
Chemart test for this entry, `test_oregonator_real_f_keeps_rate_equations`
in `tests/chemistries/test_w1_structure.py`, checks the network rather than
the dynamics: at `f = 1.5`, `k5 = 2` the reactions that consume `Z` have
total rate 2 and release `Y` at total rate 3, so a fractional `f` is
represented exactly. No test integrates the equations; the runs above are
the evidence for the window.

**Target patterns and spiral waves.** In an unstirred thin layer the BZ
reaction forms expanding rings (*target patterns*) and rotating spirals of
colour. Field's review cites Zaikin and Zhabotinsky (1970) for travelling
waves in the BZ reaction, and notes that the Oregonator's
reaction-diffusion equations support travelling waves when `X` and `Z`
diffuse at similar rates, and stationary *Turing patterns* when `Z` diffuses
faster than `X`, a case "not yet observed in the BZ reaction itself". The
book's figure 19.20 shows waves obtained with the Oregonator on a hexagonal
grid, starting from random drops of `Z`: as they spread and fill the dish,
"the positions of the original drops can still be seen". That simulation ran
on an early version of the PyCellChemistry package on top of the Breve
artificial-life simulator. Chemart does not reproduce these patterns. It
records the lattice and the diffusion coefficients in `net.extras["space"]`
but has no reaction-diffusion simulator, and the book gives neither the
diffusion coefficients nor the initial drops.

**Computing with waves.** The book's section is about *reaction-diffusion
computers* (Adamatzky et al., 2005): devices that encode
information in concentrations and compute as excitation waves travel, meet
and annihilate, much like a cellular automaton made of chemistry. The BZ
reaction is the usual medium, and the book lists what has been done with
it:

- *Image processing.* Kuhnert, Agladze and Krinsky (1989) used a
  light-sensitive BZ reaction, with a ruthenium complex as catalyst, in
  which light speeds up the production of bromide. A picture projected onto
  the dish is "stored" in the medium, which then performs contrast
  adjustment, contour detection and smoothing, all in parallel (book figure
  19.21).
- *Logic gates.* Where excitability depends on location, a pulse of
  excitation can stand for "true" and the resting state for "false"; trains
  of pulses carry bit sequences, and gates are built from colliding signals
  (Tóth and Showalter 1995; Steinbock, Kettunen and Showalter 1996; Motoike
  and Yoshikawa 1999).
- *Other algorithms.* Shortest paths in a labyrinth, Voronoi diagrams, robot
  control, a chemical memory, a chemical neuron, chemical sensors, and
  networks of BZ droplets that communicate by wave fronts.

The book also notes the limits: the computation is slow, and the BZ
reaction needs sulphuric acid, which rules out biological settings. These
are experiments with the real BZ reaction, for which the Oregonator is the
standard model; Chemart reproduces none of them.

**Two versions of the scheme.** The book's five reactions are a simplified
form of the one in Field's review. There, the autocatalytic step uses the
same reactant `A` (bromate) as reaction 1 and makes `2 Z`; reaction 5 is
`B + Z -> (f/2) Y`, where `B` is the organic fuel (malonic acid); reaction
1 also yields waste, and reaction 4 gives back some `A`. In the book, `B` feeds the autocatalytic step and
reaction 5 is `Z -> f Y`. Chemart follows the book. With `A` and `B`
buffered the two forms have the same structure, differing only in how the
constants and `Z` are scaled.
